The geopolitics behind Pakistan’s $10 billion US request. Pakistan has reportedly asked the United States for a $10 billion currency-swap facility from the US Treasury’s Exchange Stabilisation Fund. The request arrived at an extraordinary moment: the United States is at war with Iran, Pakistan has become an important channel for diplomacy between Washington and Tehran, and Islamabad is again trying to turn geopolitical relevance into economic relief . The details of the proposal remain unsettled. Its legal structure, pricing, maturity, conditions and permitted uses have not been publicly disclosed. It may not be approved, and even an approved line may never be drawn. Those qualifications matter. But they do not make the request politically unimportant. On the contrary, the very possibility of such a facility tells us something about how money and power now travel together. Pakistan already has extensive experience with bilateral financial support, most notably through its currency-swap arrangement with China. A US facility would add another layer to that relationship, placing Pakistan at the intersection of two competing monetary networks. Beijing’s swap lines support trade in renminbi, advance the currency’s internationalisation and reinforce China’s political influence. Washington’s provision of dollar liquidity sustains the dollar-centred financial order while rewarding countries that matter to US economic and strategic interests. Neither side offers liquidity in a geopolitical vacuum. Pakistan should welcome additional financial insurance, but it should not confuse access to someone else’s currency with a development strategy of its own. Not an ordinary central-bank swap A bilateral swap agreement (BSA), often called a currency-swap line, is a standing arrangement between two central banks, which are the public institutions that manage countries’ currencies and foreign-exchange reserves. “Bilateral” simply means that it involves two parties. “Swap” refers to a temporary exchange of currencies, while the “line” is the maximum amount available. Signing a $10 billion line therefore does not mean that $10 billion has been handed over or added immediately to a country’s usable reserves. It means the recipient has the right to request funds under agreed conditions. If the line is drawn, the transaction takes place in two stages. Suppose the State Bank of Pakistan needs dollars. It would provide an agreed amount of rupees to the supplying institution and receive dollars in return at an exchange rate set under the agreement. Subject to the facility’s rules, those dollars could then be used to supply domestic banks, pay for essential imports, meet external obligations or calm a disorderly foreign-exchange market. At maturity, the transaction is reversed. Pakistan returns the dollars, receives its rupees back and pays any interest or fees due. A swap is therefore neither a grant nor free money. Once drawn, it creates a liability that must be repaid. Its purpose is to bridge a temporary shortage of usable foreign currency and prevent that shortage from becoming a wider financial crisis. The precise maturity, cost, permitted uses and renewal terms vary from one agreement to another. The reported US proposal is institutionally different. Pakistan is seeking support from the Treasury’s Exchange Stabilisation Fund, not a Federal Reserve swap line. It should therefore not be presented as if Pakistan has joined the Fed’s established network of central-bank liquidity arrangements. Until the terms are public, we cannot know whether it would operate like a short-term currency swap, a balance-of-payments backstop or a more loan-like stabilisation facility. Still, the history of central-bank swaps is relevant because it reveals the politics governing access to emergency liquidity. During the 2008 global financial crisis , the Federal Reserve supplied swaps to only four emerging markets—Brazil, Mexico, Singapore and South Korea—while other requests were rejected. Aditi Sahasrabuddhe, a political scientist at Brown University, argues that the selection reflected more than financial need. The Fed favoured economies that were financially open, strategically useful and aligned with American preferences in global economic governance. When the economic case was ambiguous, political considerations helped determine who got access. Another study by Sahasrabuddhe shows that interpersonal trust among central bankers also shaped the network. Strong relationships brought access to larger or less restrictive facilities; countries outside those circles had to rely on more costly alternatives. In other words, the global financial safety net is neither universal nor politically neutral. It is partly a hierarchy of relationships. That lesson applies here. Washington does not make exceptional financial commitments merely because a country asks. If Pakistan were offered a large stabilisation facility, it would be reasonable to read it as a signal that the United States sees value in Pakistan’s economic stability and continued cooperation. Two currencies, two strategies Swap lines are often described as plumbing: technical arrangements that keep currencies and credit moving. But the provider decides where to install the pipes. For the United States, supplying dollars abroad helps preserve a system built around the dollar. The Fed’s crisis facilities protect American interests as well as foreign recipients. When dollars become scarce, overseas banks and borrowers can be forced to sell assets, default on dollar obligations or bid the dollar sharply higher. Providing liquidity contains those pressures, protects internationally exposed US financial institutions and reinforces the expectation that, in a crisis, the world still turns to the United States. The political returns can extend beyond markets. Yumi Park and Sujeong Shim find that, during the 2008 crisis, recipients of Fed swap announcements experienced an increase in government popularity while approval continued to fall in non-recipient countries. Their evidence points to exchange-rate stabilisation and greater room for expansionary policy as the mechanisms. The public may know little about the swap itself, but it notices a steadier currency and a government with more room to act. The issuer of the leading reserve currency consequently gains a form of leverage that other states cannot easily reproduce. China is trying to build some of that capacity for itself. After the global financial crisis, the People’s Bank of China rapidly expanded its swap network, helping to turn what had been a selective crisis-management tool into a much broader layer of the global financial system. By the end of 2020, an IMF study counted 91 participants and roughly $1.9 trillion in announced capacity across the worldwide bilateral-swap network. China was one of the main forces behind that expansion. Its authorities have identified three overlapping goals for Chinese facilities: promoting renminbi internationalisation, facilitating trade and investment, and providing renminbi liquidity for financial stability. Some Chinese swaps, including Pakistan’s, have also been used to address balance-of-payments pressure. This is financial statecraft. A currency becomes international not simply because a government declares it so, but because foreign firms, banks and governments can obtain and use it. Every trade payment settled in renminbi, every reserve manager willing to hold it and every central bank connected to the People’s Bank of China reduces, at the margin, dependence on dollars. China’s swaps create the institutional channels through which that change could occur. They also create political relationships. Recent research by Qi Liu, Xun Pang and James Raymond Vreeland examines 38 countries that signed swap agreements with China. On average, the authors find short-run movement towards China’s foreign-policy positions after a BSA is signed, with stronger and more persistent effects among financially vulnerable countries and governments already attracted to Chinese leadership. This does not mean every swap purchases a vote. Pakistan itself does not show a statistically identifiable post-swap shift in that study, probably because its relationship with China was already exceptionally close. The broader conclusion is nevertheless important: access to liquidity can alter a government’s incentives, especially when alternative sources are scarce. The United States and China therefore pursue different but comparable forms of monetary power. China wants to make the renminbi more usable and embed its partners in a China-centred network. The United States wants to preserve the dollar’s central role and retain influence over strategically significant states. A swap may be denominated in currency, but it is also denominated in trust, access and expectations about future cooperation. Why Pakistan matters now Pakistan’s reported request cannot be separated from the war with Iran. Islamabad has served as a mediator and a venue for US-Iran contacts, giving it a role neither Washington nor Tehran can easily dismiss. Its geography connects South Asia, China, Iran, Afghanistan and the Arabian Sea. Its military relationships with Gulf states, long partnership with China and ability to communicate across rival camps make it unusually useful during a regional conflict. For Washington, a financially stable and cooperative Pakistan can help sustain diplomacy, limit wider regional escalation and prevent Beijing from becoming Islamabad’s only dependable source of emergency support. A Treasury facility would also remind Pakistani elites that access to the dollar system can deliver benefits that the renminbi cannot yet fully match. The strategic message would be clear: Pakistan still has a place within the American orbit. For Pakistan, the attraction is obvious. A large dollar backstop could reassure markets, reduce the fear of an abrupt external-financing crisis and give the State Bank more room to manage volatility. Even an undrawn line may convey confidence. Pakistan has simultaneously been reducing near-term foreign liabilities, seeking longer-tenor financing and preparing a return to international capital markets. A credible backstop could reinforce those efforts by reducing rollover risk and reassuring lenders that Pakistan can meet its near-term dollar obligations. The timing supports a geopolitical interpretation, but it does not prove a quid pro quo. No public evidence shows that Washington has offered $10 billion in exchange for a specified Pakistani position on Iran, China or any other issue. Nor is approval guaranteed. Pakistan’s own history should caution against treating temporary strategic attention as a durable economic alliance. American interest has repeatedly risen and fallen with wars and crises in the region. Islamabad should also resist the temptation to convert its mediating role into participation in someone else’s war. Its economic interest lies in de-escalation. Conflict with neighbouring Iran would create security risks, disrupt energy and trade, strain domestic cohesion and compromise Pakistan’s ability to work with China and the Gulf states. The value Pakistan currently offers Washington is precisely its ability to communicate across dividing lines. Sacrificing that position would destroy the asset it is trying to monetise. Liquidity is not development The financial benefits of swap lines are real, but easily overstated. An undrawn facility is contingent financing, not an addition to usable foreign-exchange reserves. Once drawn, a swap creates a future repayment obligation. Repeated rollovers can make a short-term liquidity instrument resemble long-term debt, while allowing governments to advertise stronger headline reserves than their net position warrants. The Chinese experience demonstrates the risks. Pakistan signed its swap agreement with China in December 2011 and began drawing on it in 2013. The IMF found that Pakistan and Mongolia accounted for much of the approximately $8 billion outstanding under China’s overseas swaps at the end of 2020. The arrangement gave Pakistan breathing space and supported the use of regional currencies in trade. Yet the liquidity was not equivalent to unrestricted dollars. A recent working paper explains why markets have become more cautious about Chinese swaps. Renminbi cannot automatically service dollar-denominated sovereign debt. Conversion may introduce additional cost, exchange-rate risk and negotiation. Important conditions governing drawdown and convertibility are often opaque. In Pakistan’s case, experience showed that repayment in renminbi could become costly as the rupee depreciated. The authors find that Pakistan’s 2011 signing was initially followed by narrower bond spreads, but the reassuring effect of Chinese BSAs generally weakened over time as investors learned about their operational limits. This is not an argument against the Chinese facility. It is an argument for matching the instrument to the need. Renminbi liquidity is most useful for settling eligible imports from China, supporting bilateral trade and reducing the need to obtain dollars for those transactions. Dollar liquidity is more useful for dollar debts and for stabilising markets that still price risk in dollars. Pakistan can benefit from both, provided it does not pretend that the currencies are interchangeable or that either arrangement fixes structural weaknesses. The IMF study reaches the same sober conclusion: swap lines are now a valuable part of the global financial safety net, but there is little evidence that they automatically improve macroeconomic policy. They may even delay adjustment when governments use temporary liquidity to postpone necessary reform. Pakistan needs a swap strategy If the US proposal advances, Pakistan should negotiate and use it according to a publicly stated framework. First, the government should disclose the essentials: the facility’s legal form, currency, interest rate, maturity, renewal provisions, permitted uses, drawdown conditions and relationship to existing IMF commitments. The same transparency should apply to Chinese swaps. Markets cannot treat a backstop as fully credible when they do not know whether it can be used. Second, Islamabad should treat swaps as insurance, not income. Drawings should be triggered by genuine liquidity stress, disorderly currency conditions or clearly identified external payments, not by a desire to finance an import-led consumption boom. Gross reserves, net reserves and swap liabilities should be reported separately so the public can see what the State Bank owns and what it owes. Third, each currency should be used where it is most effective. Renminbi drawings should primarily support trade and obligations to China, while Pakistan should seek the broadest feasible convertibility and least costly repayment terms. Any US facility should strengthen the reserve buffer and smooth temporary dollar shortages, not underwrite an artificially strong rupee. Fourth, the breathing space must finance adjustment in the broad sense, not defer it. Pakistan’s chronic dollar shortage reflects a narrow export base, costly energy dependence, and recurrent import-led growth. Liquidity can buy time for export upgrading, energy reform, productivity-enhancing investment and better domestic revenue mobilisation. It cannot substitute for them. Finally, Pakistan should avoid allowing either facility to become an exclusive strategic claim. Maintaining access to both networks can increase national autonomy, but only if Islamabad is prepared to say no when financial support comes with policies contrary to Pakistan’s development interests. Diversification is valuable because it creates options, not because it permits the country to auction its foreign policy to the highest bidder. The proposed $10 billion US facility could be useful. So is Pakistan’s established swap relationship with China. But their greatest value would lie in helping Pakistan escape the cycle in which every reserve crisis produces another emergency request and every geopolitical crisis produces another temporary windfall. Washington and Beijing will continue to use money in pursuit of power. Pakistan’s task is to use their money in pursuit of development. Norway commends Pakistan's 'constructive role' in US-Iran conflict. Norway on Thursday commended Pakistan’s “important and constructive role” to mediate between the United States and Iran amid the Middle East conflict. The development came as Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar held delegation-level talks with Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide, who arrived in Islamabad earlier in the day, the first such visit in a decade. “Both sides reviewed the whole gamut of bilateral cooperation in various fields, including trade, investment, climate change, maritime affairs and education. They recognised the important role of the Pakistani diaspora in Norway and agreed to strengthen people-to-people ties between the two countries,” the Foreign Office (FO) said. The two sides expressed satisfaction at the warm and cordial state of Pakistan-Norway relations and agreed to further deepen cooperation in areas of mutual interest,” it said. The FO said the two sides also held in-depth discussions on regional and international developments of mutual interest. “The Norwegian foreign minister commended Pakistan’s important and constructive role during the recent Iran-US conflict, including the leadership and contributions of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, DPM Dar and Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir,” it said. In televised remarks, Eide appreciated Pakistan’s efforts to promote peace and expressed Norway’s desire to further strengthen bilateral ties. He said Norway and Pakistan had a “very strong bilateral partnership”, adding that the presence of a large Pakistani community in Norway, which was “well integrated into Norwegian society”, had helped strengthen ties between the two countries. “There are many leading politicians in Norway and many close colleagues who are actually of Pakistani-Norwegian descent, so it has really made a mark,” he said. Eide said business ties between the two countries were also growing, particularly in the energy and fertiliser sectors, with Norwegian companies increasingly looking at opportunities in Pakistan. He said Norway also saw opportunities for Pakistan to strengthen economic relations through its cooperation with Switzerland and Iceland, noting that the three countries could provide further avenues for expanding business relations. Turning to the regional situation, Eide strongly commended the actions taken by Pakistan’s leadership, including the prime minister and foreign minister, in efforts to promote peace in the Middle East. Eide described the ongoing war as “incredibly dangerous” for global peace as well as the world economy, and praised Pakistan for stepping forward. He also appreciated Pakistan’s role in facilitating the Islamabad talks and maintaining engagement with the parties involved. “I think it is fair to say that the position of Pakistan on the world stage, also in peacemaking, has really been strengthened by this commitment,” he said. Eide said Norway was ready to assist Pakistan’s peace efforts, noting that Oslo had experience in peace negotiations and maintained open dialogue with both Tehran and Washington. “Wherever we can be useful, we will,” he said. He also highlighted Norway’s experience in international maritime affairs, saying the country was among the world’s major seafaring nations despite its relatively small population. He said Norway could therefore play a constructive role in discussions concerning international maritime law and developments surrounding the Strait of Hormuz. Dar, Eide discuss bilateral ties Earlier, the two ministers held a “restricted-format meeting”. “DPM Dar warmly welcomed Eide to Pakistan. The two ministers discussed the full range of bilateral relations, as well as regional and international developments, and reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation in all areas of mutual interest,” it said. Upon his arrival in Islamabad, Eide was received at the airport by Additional Foreign Secretary (Europe) Ambassador Ayesha Ali. In a statement on Wednesday, the FO said the minister is undertaking the visit from Aug 13-14 at Dar’s invitation. During the visit, the two will hold delegation-level talks covering the full spectrum of Pakistan-Norway relations, it said. “The two sides will discuss avenues for further expanding bilateral cooperation, particularly in trade and investment, climate change, renewable energy, education and people-to-people contacts. “They will also exchange views on important regional and international developments,” it added. It said that the visit would build on high-level engagement between the two countries, including phone conversation between Dar and Eide in March and April , and the visit of Norway’s State Secretary Andreas Motzfeldt Kravik to Islamabad in May. The FO stated that the visit would provide an opportunity to “further strengthen the longstanding and cordial relations between Pakistan and Norway and to explore new areas of mutually beneficial cooperation”.

SHC orders formation of committee to probe HIV outbreak among children at Karachi hospital. KARACHI: The Sindh High Court (SHC) directed the provincial government on Thursday to constitute a committee for an “independent, impartial and comprehensive” inquiry into the HIV outbreak among children at Karachi’s Kulsum Bai Valika Hospital. A two-member SHC bench, headed by Justice Adnanul Karim Memon and comprising Justice Muhammad Jaffer Raza, issued the directive as it announced its reserved judgement on a plea seeking an independent inquiry, registration of a case and lifelong medical treatment as well as appropriate compensation for the affected children. The outbreak was initially reported late last year, following which the Sindh government carried out screening at the Sindh Employees Social Security Institution-run hospital located in Karachi’s SITE area. According to data shared by the Sindh government, at least 78 children have been found infected with HIV at the hospital while a screening in the nearby area also confirmed 120 additional cases. But Advocate Tariq Mansoor, the lawyer who moved the SHC on the matter, claimed in his petition filed in May that the total number of infected children is around 200. The court observed in its order on the plea that the departmental proceedings and reports submitted so far had been “insufficient to determine the number of affected persons, the source and circumstances of transmission, compliance with infection-control protocols and the Sindh Regulation and Control of Disposable Syringes Act, 2010, as well as the supervisory and individual responsibility of the officials concerned”. Keeping this in view, the court deemed it necessary “in the interest of justice, transparency and public confidence that an independent fact-finding mechanism be constituted by the competent authority, without expressing any final opinion regarding the guilt or innocence of any individual”. It directed that a committee, headed by the Sindh chief secretary, be constituted. The chief secretary should co-opt two senior officers not below the rank of BS-20 and “preferably having no direct administrative involvement in the affairs of the hospital or the proceedings under inquiry” to join the committee, the court order stated. The court directed that the committee should determine: The actual number and particulars of children and other patients who were found HIV-positive and who received treatment at the hospital during the relevant period The source, circumstances and possible mode of transmission of HIV infection, based on available medical and scientific evidence Whether any disposable syringe or other medical equipment was reused, improperly disposed of, inadequately sterilised or otherwise used in violation of the applicable law, rules, protocols or standard medical practice The existence and implementation of infection-prevention and control protocols at the hospital The procurement, supply, storage, distribution and use of auto-lock, auto-destruct or auto-break syringes and the relevant record The role and responsibility of medical, nursing, technical, administrative and supervisory officials concerned Whether any officer or official, by act or omission, failed to discharge a statutory, administrative or supervisory duty The status and legality of the departmental proceedings already initiated against the 37 officials and whether such proceedings adequately address the actual responsibility of the persons concerned Whether any provision of the Sindh Regulation and Control of Disposable Syringes Act, 2010, or any other applicable law has been violated and, if so, the persons prima facie responsible The measures required for preventing recurrence of any such incident in the future The court order further stated that the committee should be empowered to examine all relevant records, including medical and laboratory reports, screening data, procurement and stock registers, syringe records, duty rosters, infection-control and inspection reports, inquiry proceedings, CCTV footage where such incidents occurred in Sindh and other material necessary for an “objective determination, while affording a fair opportunity of hearing to any person against whom an adverse finding is proposed”. The committee should submit its comprehensive report to the competent authority, as well as the SHC, within two months of its constitution, the order read. It elaborated that the report should identify “the factual position and, where supported by evidence, fixing responsibility and recommending appropriate departmental, statutory or criminal action pursuant to Section 7 of the Sindh Regulation and Control of Disposable Syringes Act, 2010”. Pending the inquiry, the Sindh chief secretary should ensure through the relevant departments and SESSI that all affected HIV-positive children and other identified patients receive “comprehensive, uninterrupted and appropriate medical treatment”, including medicines, investigations, counselling and follow-up care, entirely free of cost, at any institution of higher standard as medically appropriate, the court ruled. “All such expenses shall be borne by the government/ SESSI and shall not be recovered from the affected patients or their families, and the arrangement shall continue for as long as medically required,” the court directed. Noting the “extraordinary circumstances of the case and the vulnerability of the affected children”, the court further directed the provincial chief secretary to determine and process the “entitlement of each affected child/ family to compensation, financial assistance or other lawful relief, strictly in accordance with the applicable statutory framework and government policy”. The chief secretary should ensure that the process is completed expeditiously and without unnecessary hardship to the affected families, the order said. Moreover, the relevant authorities should ensure that no affected child or family is discriminated against, stigmatised or denied medical, social or other lawful assistance on account of HIV status, the court ruled, adding that the identity and medical information of affected children should be dealt with strictly in accordance with applicable law and accepted medical standards relating to confidentiality. The court further directed the chief secretary and the health department secretary to ensure immediate preventive and corrective measures at Kulsum Bai Valika Hospital to eliminate any further avoidable risk to patients and strict compliance with the Sindh Regulation and Control of Disposable Syringes Act, 2010, infection-prevention protocols and other applicable health regulations. Where necessary, they should also ensure the framing of requisite rules in accordance with law, the court order added. The court also observed that the matter concerned the protection of the rights to life, health, dignity and fair treatment and warranted an independent, transparent and evidence-based inquiry. “The matter cannot be treated merely as an administrative issue, as the constitutional obligation to protect life under Article 9 [of the Constitution] extends to ensuring effective discharge of public-health and medical-safety responsibilities, particularly towards vulnerable patients,” the court order read. However, it added, “allegations or departmental proceedings cannot by themselves establish individual culpability, which must be determined based on evidence and after due opportunity of hearing”. Beyond FOI: Why permission-based transparency fails the public. Imagine an ordinary citizen trying to track flood-control spending in their province. They want to cross-examine project costs, contractors, locations, and completion rates — not as professional investigative journalists, but as community members whose neighborhoods submerge under water every monsoon season despite billions in public allocations. Yet, under the current Freedom of Information (FOI) paradigm, accessing this data remains an uphill battle. In September 2025, a citizen requested flood-control project data from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in structured CSV or Excel format. The official response noted that no flood-control map database was available on the agency's website, leaving the requester with no option but to appeal. In another case, the DPWH approved a project-list request — only to instruct the citizen to check their private email for the data. According to Ann Cuisia, Founder and CEO of TraXion Tech, this dynamic highlights a structural flaw in how the government handles public records. She emphasizes that transparency should not depend on belonging to a media organization or having the resources to fight through bureaucracy. When people have no data, they have no practical tool to question power, and corruption thrives where evidence is hardest to see. Under traditional permission-based transparency mechanisms like standard FOI, a citizen must file an explicit request, undergo agency review, navigate processing wait periods or potential fees, and ultimately receive a one-time static document or private email transmission. In contrast, a modern disclosure-by-default framework hosts centralized open data portals publishing standardized CSV files, JSON feeds, and open APIs, which enables instant downloads and continuous analysis for any member of the public without administrative friction. The Pitfalls of Permission-Based Transparency The core issue lies in permission-based transparency. Even when public records are eventually released, they rarely form a searchable, reusable public dataset. The next citizen seeking the exact same information must start the bureaucratic loop all over again — registering, submitting government identification, navigating agency jurisdictions, and waiting for approval. In addition, while filing an FOI request is legally free, several citizens requesting government-held datasets have reported being redirected to third-party services that require processing fees. This raises a fundamental question about why citizens should pay twice for non-confidential data that was already collected, processed, and maintained using public tax funds. Disclosure by Default: The Global Standard Other nations have long transitioned to proactive disclosure by default. In the United Kingdom, all Cabinet Office spending transactions exceeding £25,000 are automatically published as downloadable CSV files. On a broader scale, public procurement notices globally are increasingly published in standardized JSON via open APIs under the Open Contracting Data Standard. This enables researchers, civic technologists, and ordinary residents to analyze government spending continuously without seeking permission, submitting ID, or explaining why they need the data. The Philippines actually adopted open data principles as far back as 2015, mandating that government datasets be publicly accessible by default, machine-readable, openly licensed, and regularly updated. While the policy framework exists on paper, the administrative culture and enforcement mechanisms have lagged far behind. The Real-World Cost of Broken Data This lack of structured data carries severe real-world consequences. Without standardized, machine-readable records, watchdog organizations and citizens cannot easily run automated checks to flag duplicated projects across agency dockets, unusual pricing anomalies or bid padding, recurring contractors despite poor performance histories, and full disbursements for incomplete or ghost infrastructure projects. “Public records should be open unless a specific lawful exception applies, such as national security, personal privacy or an ongoing investigation. FOI must remain available for exceptional requests. But it should never substitute for government’s duty to publish,” Cuisia added.

Tiangco not complacent despite success of Navotas flood control system. Navotas City lone district Rep. Toby Tiangco refuses to be complacent despite the apparent effectiveness of the city's flood control system amid the Habagat-strengthened rains in the metropolis. Despite days of persistent rainfall, the city's navigational gate, coastal dike, flood gates, concrete box culverts, and network of pumping stations have been working in unison to keep floodwaters under control. This has prevented seawater from entering communities during high tide while efficiently draining rainwater from city streets. "Hindi pa kumpleto ang proyektong ito. Marami pa tayong kailangang gawin at ayusin. Hindi tayo titigil sa paghahanap ng mga paraan upang lalo pang maprotektahan ang ating mga kababayan," Tiangco said on Thursday, Aug 13. (This project is not yet complete. We still have much to do and fix. We will not stop seeking ways to further protect our people.) For one of the country's lowest-lying coastal cities—surrounded by Manila Bay and the Navotas-Malabon River and crisscrossed by approximately 15 kilometers of waterways—effective flood management is not a luxury but a necessity. In particular, the navigational gate regulates tidal waters to prevent seawater from flowing into the Navotas-Malabon River during high tide. Unsatisfied, Tiangco has set his sights on a second navigational gate. "Sa ngayon ang pinaka-importante dito ay ang pangalawang navigational gate, dahil ang kasalukyang navigational gate ay luma na, may mga abnormal na tunog at naapawan na ng tubig kapag malakas ang alon," he said. (For now, the most important part is the second navigational gate, because the current one is old, produces abnormal sounds, and gets flooded when waves are strong.) "Pag sira ang navigational gate, bali wala na ang lahat ng ibang bahagi ng flood control system natin dahil tagos ang tubig hight tide, kaya dapat magkaroon ng back na bagong navigational gate," the veteran lawmaker stressed. (If the navigational gate fails, the entire flood control system becomes useless since water passes through at high tide, so a new backup navigational gate must be built.) He says the Habagat rains serve as another demonstration that when government projects are well-conceived, properly implemented, and consistently maintained, they continue to protect communities for generations . The city's coastal dike serves as a barrier against storm surges and tidal flooding from Manila Bay, while strategically operated flood gates allow the passage of municipal fishing boats during low tide before closing ahead of high tide. Complementing these are the city's pumping stations, which continuously remove accumulated rainwater, and underground concrete box culverts beneath major roads that temporarily impound and channel excess water. These interconnected systems must all function together for the city's flood defenses to be effective. Tiangco vowed to continue to work and invest in projects that provide stronger protection for his constituents "Hangad natin na dumating ang panahon na ang bawat Navoteño ay makapamuhay nang malaya sa takot na dulot ng pagbaha sa tuwing may malakas na ulan o mataas na tubig," he said. (We hope for the time when every Navoteño can live free from the fear of flooding during heavy rains or high water.)

Muntinlupa signs 4Ps data-sharing accord with DSWD-NCR. The Muntinlupa City government and the Department of Social Welfare and Development–National Capital Region (DSWD-NCR) have signed a data-sharing agreement to hasten and improve the delivery of services to beneficiaries of the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps). Muntinlupa Mayor Ruffy Biazon and Michael Joseph Lorico, regional director of the DSWD Field Office NCR, formalized the agreement. Currently, 4,297 households across eight barangays in Muntinlupa are enrolled in 4Ps, which provides financial assistance to poor families. The agreement aims to enhance case management and speed up the identification of beneficiaries’ needs. These include additional support for health and nutrition, appropriate assistance in education, livelihood assessments for potential training beneficiaries, and immediate emergency response. Through the data-sharing initiative, programs and services can be better targeted and focused on families most in need.

More than 6,500 families in Calumpit, Bulacan received relief goods from the provincial government on Wednesday, August 12, as floodwaters continued to swamp the town. Gov. Daniel R. Fernando, Vice Gov. Alex Castro, Provincial Social Welfare and Development Office (PSWDO) head Rowena J. Tiongson, and First District Board Member Mina Fermin led the distribution, joined by Mayor Lem Faustino, Vice Mayor Zacarias Candelaria, and members of the Sangguniang Bayan. Residents from the hardest-hit barangays Gatbuca, San Miguel, and Meysulao were among those given food packs and supplies. Police personnel under Bulacan Provincial Police Director Col. Jay Baybayin and Calumpit police chief Lt. Col. Leopold Estorque helped secure the operation, alongside disaster response officers from the Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO). Flooding has affected 29 barangays, displacing 154,961 individuals from 46,498 families. Nineteen evacuation centers are sheltering 845 families, while several roads remain impassable, with others only accessible to large vehicles, according to the Calumpit MDRRMO.

CinePanalo expands reach, brings Filipino stories to more audiences. The opportunity to experience original Filipino narratives in theaters is becoming increasingly rare, with only a handful of producers and investors willing to take a chance on homegrown productions. It is therefore encouraging to see festivals like Puregold’s CinePanalo working to bring Filipino films to wider audiences. This year, the festival will screen seven full-length films and 20 student-made shorts at select Ayala Malls Cinemas across Metro Manila, including Market! Market! in Taguig, TriNoma and Fairview Terraces in Quezon City, Ayala Malls Feliz in Pasig, Ayala Malls Manila Bay in Parañaque, and Ayala Malls Circuit in Makati. For a festival built around Filipino stories and emerging filmmakers, the expanded theatrical presence is particularly significant. It gives filmmakers more opportunities to connect with audiences while allowing viewers to discover stories and perspectives that may otherwise have limited space in commercial theaters. “Partnering with Ayala Malls helps bring the 2026 CinePanalo to as many Filipinos as possible,” said Puregold Senior Marketing Manager Ivy Hayagan-Piedad. “As the festival continues to grow, we truly value partnerships like this that stand by the cause of unleashing Filipino cinema’s untapped potential.” Ayala Malls’ Head of Ancillary Business Yvette Roldan said the festival’s focus on Filipino audiences and filmmakers was among the reasons for the partnership. “CinePanalo’s advocacy greatly aligns with Ayala Malls’ vision and values,” Roldan said, citing the festival’s focus on stories that reflect Filipino lives and experiences. Now in its third edition, CinePanalo continues to create opportunities for Filipino films to reach audiences, bringing homegrown stories to more viewers and giving them the chance to experience these narratives where they belong: on the big screen.

Lacson files bills seeking to raise retirement age for PNP, BJMP, BFP personnel to 57. Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson has filed two measures seeking to raise the compulsory retirement age for personnel of the Philippine National Police (PNP) as well as the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) and Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) from 56 to 57. In filing Senate Bill Nos. 2395 and 2396, Lacson proposed adjusting the age of retirement to allow the three agencies to maximize the expertise, leadership and institutional knowledge of their senior officers, while giving them more time to pass these on to younger personnel. “This bill, which seeks to increase the retirement age of the members of the PNP to fifty-seven (57) years old, intends to give the PNP leadership more time to implement their intended institutional reforms and for the institution to maximize the years-worth of knowledge and skills of their personnel,” Lacson said in SB No. 2395, which seeks to increase the retirement age for PNP uniformed personnel from 56 to 57. The senator also said SB No. 2396, which similarly seeks to increase the compulsory retirement age for BJMP and BFP members to 57, aims “to give the senior officers of the BJMP and BFP the opportunity to maximize their expertise, leadership, and institutional knowledge while providing additional time to impart the same to the younger officers of the bureau.” Both measures are also aligned with the adjustment in the compulsory retirement age of members of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP). Lacson, who served as Chief, PNP from 1999 to 2001, noted that the PNP currently has 230,410 uniformed personnel while the BJMP has 26,000 staff and the BFP has 41,286 personnel. Also, SB 2395 seeks to amend the retirement age for PNP uniformed personnel to "age fifty-seven (57)." But “uniformed personnel who have less than one year in the service upon the effectivity of this act shall have the option to retire at the age of 56, and shall be considered compulsorily retired (and) that the incumbent Chief of the PNP shall be compulsorily retired at the age of fifty-six (56).” Senate Bill 2396, meanwhile, seeks to include BJMP and BFP uniformed personnel among those whose compulsory retirement age would be 57. However, under the proposed amendment, however, “in case of any officer with the rank of chief superintendent, director, or deputy director general, the Commission may allow his retention in the service for an unextendible period of one year.”

Gong Yoo bids farewell to his cat of 15 Years: 'Thank you, see you again'. Korean actor Gong Yoo has said goodbye to his beloved longtime cat, whom he considered family and held close to his heart. The “Goblin” actor shared a heartfelt farewell on social media, accompanied by photos of him with his cat, Kongkong. “Because you were my first, I cared about you even more, and I liked that you were like me, though I don't know how you felt,” Gong Yoo wrote. He added, “Thank you for staying by my side for so long. Let’s meet again for sure. I miss you.” Though brief, his message conveyed the depth of his grief over losing a companion who had been part of his life for many years. The photos showed Gong Yoo spending quiet moments with Kongkong, including one of the cat resting comfortably on his lap as the actor gazed at him affectionately. Fans expressed their condolences and sent messages of comfort to the actor as they mourned the loss alongside him. Gong Yoo has long been known for his love of animals and has shared glimpses of his life with his pets over the years. His farewell to Kongkong, particularly his promise that they would meet again, struck an especially emotional chord with fans.

Philippines races to rebuild nuclear expertise as atomic energy plans advance. The Philippines needs to rebuild its pool of nuclear-trained workers as it moves closer to developing nuclear power, with many local experts having either retired or taken their skills overseas, according to state-run National Power Corp. (Napocor). Following a recent meeting with the Vienna-based International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Napocor President and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Jericho Nograles said workforce development should be a top priority as the country works to meet 19 infrastructure requirements for nuclear energy development. “Many of our nuclear-trained personnel have since retired. Others took their expertise overseas, where Filipino engineers and skilled workers have contributed to nuclear facilities around the world,” Nograles told a press briefing, noting that about 80 percent of the workers at Barakah nuclear facility in United Arab Emirates (UAE) are Filipinos. Apart from human resource (HR) development, the other areas that the Philippines needs to address are national position, nuclear safety, management, funding and financing, legal framework, safeguards, regulatory framework, radiation protection, electrical grid, stakeholder involvement, site and supporting facilities, environmental protection, emergency planning, nuclear security, nuclear fuel cycle, radioactive waste management, industrial involvement, and procurement. The Department of Energy (DOE) recently met with the IAEA to address these key infrastructure requirements. The IAEA noted that the Philippines is ready to advance to the second phase of its nuclear energy roadmap, following the first phase’s focus on foundational policy and planning considerations. The government has already laid some groundwork through Executive Order (EO) No. 116, which focuses on nuclear energy studies, and EO 164, which mandated the DOE to include nuclear energy in the generation mix. Furthermore, the country has already signed the 123 Agreement for civilian nuclear cooperation with the United States (US) and is partnering with South Korea to assess the viability of rehabilitating Bataan Nuclear Power Plant (BNPP), which was initially constructed under Napocor. Meanwhile, the second phase is set to focus on infrastructure development that would allow the government to invite bids or negotiate project contracts. Under this phase, the DOE is looking at potential funding and financing pathways, such as public-private partnerships (PPPs), consortium arrangements, and build-own-operate models, among others. The DOE is also looking at finalizing the third phase of its nuclear roadmap, which focuses on preparing the country for nuclear commissioning and operations. So far, the agency has identified Bataan, Palawan, Masbate, Pangasinan, and Camarines Norte provinces as initial areas for potential power plant sites. While these locations are subject to further assessment, DOE Undersecretary Giovanni Bacordo said nuclear power plant construction is just one part of the country’s integration of nuclear energy. “Nuclear energy is not simply about deciding to build a power plant. We must build the institutions, the regulatory system, the technical capability, the financing framework, and the public confidence to support it. Our progress shows that the Philippines is putting those foundations in place,” Bacordo said.

Damage to infrastructure, agriculture hits P3 B as habagat continues to bring more rains. The damage to infrastructure and agriculture wrought by heavy rains due to tropical two cyclones and southwest monsoon reached around P3 billion as a result of widespread flooding and other adverse effects of the downpour. As of Thursday morning, Aug 13, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC), said the damage to infrastructure is now at around P2.65 billion after bridges and road networks were affected. The agricultural damage is currently at P347 million. The figures were based on the latest assessment of the impact of tropical cyclones “Luis” and “Maymay”, as well as the southwest monsoon (habagat), which has been continuously inducing heavy rains in various parts of Luzon and the Visayas. The bad news, however, is that the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said that habagat will continue to bring rains over Luzon and parts of Western Visayas. Occasional moderate to heavy rains may persist in Zambales and Bataan. Meanwhile, cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms may prevail over Metro Manila, Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region, Cagayan Valley, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Rizal, Quezon, Oriental Mindoro, Occidental Mindoro, Marinduque, Romblon, Palawan, the rest of Central Luzon, Camarines Norte, Aklan, Antique, and Capiz. PAGASA weather specialist Leanne Loreto warned that the monsoon rains could trigger flooding and landslides, particularly in areas that have received significant rainfall in the past few days. 26 dead In its data, the Office of Civil Defense (OCD) recorded 21 fatalities, all of them are still for validation. The Philippine National Police (PNP), however, said the death toll from the three weather disturbances is now 26, most of them due to landslides including the incident in Baguio City that left 16 people dead. Seven fatalities were reported in Batangas and Rizal while one each in Pangasinan and La Union. Also included in the fatality list was the policeman who drowned in Negros Island Region while trying to save his two police buddies. Two people are still on the missing list in Calabarzon while the PNP also recorded 15 injured. Displaced The weather disturbances also displaced more than 15,000 families composed of 53,570 people who are still staying in various evacuation centers in 10 regions. They are part of the 1.087 million families, composed of 3.7 million individuals who were affected by the heavy rains. The OCD also reported a total of 1,336 partially damaged houses and 103 totally damaged houses, mostly due to widespread flooding. So far, the national government has provided over P458 million in assistance packages to the affected residents.

Teen found dead after river mishap in Bulacan; 3 still missing. The body of one of four missing teenagers swept away by strong currents in the Marilao River was recovered Wednesday night, Aug. 12, in Sitio Kaybanban, Barangay Parada, Santa Maria, Bulacan. Authorities said the victim, a 17‑year‑old boy, was identified by his family. His body, swollen and barely recognizable, was retrieved by rescuers from San Jose del Monte who failed to coordinate with the Santa Maria Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office. The youths reportedly jumped into the river in Barangay Gayagaya, San Jose del Monte, on Monday, Aug. 10, daring each other to cross despite warnings from barangay personnel about rising waters. Witnesses said the group briefly left the area but returned to continue the challenge before being swept away. Search and retrieval operations for the three other missing boys are ongoing, with local governments of San Jose del Monte and Caloocan, the Coast Guard Auxiliary, and Bulacan rescue teams working together.

‘Made by Google’ event reveals the new Pixel 11 phones and other hardware. Google has announced four new Pixel phones, if you’ve been keeping tabs on them for a while, then you’d know they are: The Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold (Why they continue to this the Pro Fold is beyond me). They have also announced the Pixel Watch and the Pixel Tag. New to the Pixel phones is the HiLight. It is the light fixture in the camera bump, which is designed for two things. The first, is to let you know Gemini is listening–actively, at least. And the second, is to let you know that a favorite contact is reaching out–this way, if your phone buzzes, you can ignore it if it’s someone you deem unimportant (LOL). The hardware aspect of these devices are nothing to write about. Sure, they use a Tensor G6 processor, which we can guess is probably fifteen to twenty percent more efficient. Their screens have about 3000 or more nits of brightness, which is only ever really useful while outdoors against the sun. You’d probably never want 3000 nits of brightness in the middle of the night. That would be like getting banished to the Shadow Realm, Seto Kaiba style (Yugioh, anyone? Can’t be that old, am I?). Instead, Google does what Google does best, which is software development. The Pixel phones are running on Android 17 and get the full support of Gemini, which Google is now dubbing Gemini Intelligence. This includes AI agents that can book rides. So, imagine launching Gemini to tell it to book you a ride to your destination, without you launching the app itself and typing in where you need to go. Google says Gemini Intelligence will be capable of doing things, thanks to its contextual awareness. For instance, it can read your Gmail, and understand you need certain things, and it will add them in your shopping cart. It can check your calendar and let you know if you would be available on free dates when you get messages of friends wanting to hang out. It’s all about saving a minute or two of your time, to do something else, I suppose, like, doomscroll. Rather, it’s all about doing things for you so you don’t have to, think, about it. Rambler is also a new feature, which lets you record your voice to text, and it can automatically remove filler words, like all those ums and, like, you know, just the words that anyone typically mutters when vocally forming their sentences. Circle to Search is available through the camera app. So you can just point at something and circle to search it, without the need to actually capture a photo. There is also a new thing called Magic Capture, which captures videos and photos of “moments,” which Google says allows users to “live it.” For instance, concerts, so you don’t have to stare at the phone when My Chemical Romance arrives later this year, as the Magic Capture will automatically capture and clean it up for you. Then there’s Camera Looks, which is basically a set of filters based on films. This was probably born out of that attempt to replicate a Wes Anderson color-style that blew up a few years ago. Perhaps one of the new things introduced in the Pixel 11 series that is genuinely impressive and useful is the sign-to-text. This is sign language. The Pixel phone can translate sign language into texts, which makes communication accessible for people who use it. I cannot wait for this feature to expand to other devices, because this is actually a solution to a problem. It’s something some users may never get to use, but the option for it to be there is very much a welcomed one. The Pixel Watch 5 specs sheet, like the phones, we can view as being fifteen or twenty percent more capable. Google says Pixel Watch 5 can track blood oxygen and insulin resistance, and improved sleep tracking data. And finally, the new Google product, the Pixel Tag, which is a bluetooth tracker. You can track it not just with your Android device but also through your Pixel Watch. This can be handy for travellers to keep track of your belongings. Officially there is no Google store available in the Philippines. But we’ll be keeping track of stores that sells them locally if you want to check them out for yourself.

Quezon City patrol cops arrest teen with revolver. A 19-year-old man was arrested after a police officer spotted a loaded revolver tucked into his waist during an anti-criminality patrol in Barangay Greater Fairview, Quezon City, Wednesday evening, Aug. 12. At around 6 p.m., a barker-dispatcher approached the police officer and reported that a man had allegedly pointed a firearm at him while he was working. The complainant pointed to the suspect, identified as alias “Jo,” who was seated inside a makeshift shelter made of cardboard boxes in front of an abandoned building on Commonwealth Avenue. Upon approaching Jo, the officer instructed him to raise his shirt, revealing the firearm tucked into his waist. Police immediately arrested Jo and confiscated an Armscor revolver loaded with three live rounds of .38-caliber ammunition. Jo, a resident of Barangay Pasong Putik, Quezon City, is facing charges of grave threats under Article 282 of the Revised Penal Code and violation of Republic Act No. 10591, or the Comprehensive Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act. The charges are being prepared for filing at the Quezon City Prosecutor’s Office.

Police probes man’s death in Pasay. Police in Pasay are investigating the case of an unidentified man who was discovered lifeless at a street corner in Barangay 76 early Thursday, Aug. 13, after witnesses said he had vomited blood the night before. Pasay City Police chief Col. Joselito De Sesto said the victim, later identified only by the alias “Tropa,” was about 60 to 65 years old, 5’5” to 5’7” tall, slim, and fair-skinned. He was wearing green jersey shorts and a long-sleeved shirt when found. The body was discovered around 6:30 a.m. at the corner of Libertad Channel and Diokno Boulevard. A witness told police the man had been seen vomiting blood around 9 p.m. Wednesday. Residents tried to offer him food, but he refused and eventually lay down. By morning, he was unresponsive and no longer breathing. Responding officers from Sub-Station 1 and Scene of the Crime Operations (SOCO) personnel found no external injuries. Investigators said the death may have been due to natural causes, possibly tuberculosis, based on the reported symptoms. The remains were brought to Veronica Funeral Homes for safekeeping. Police said further examination will be conducted to determine the exact cause of death.

CHED allocates ₱56.66 million for medical technology, pharmacy student scholarships. The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) has allocated ₱56.66 million from the Higher Education Development Fund (HEDF) to sustain scholarships for students pursuing medical technology and pharmacy. The funding will cover the financial requirements of existing scholars under the Scholarship Program for Future Medical Technologists and Pharmacists (MTP-SP), allowing them to continue their studies through Academic Year 2026-2027. CHED said the program covers 238 ongoing scholars for the second semester of AY 2025-2026 and 300 scholars for the first semester of AY 2026-2027. The Commission said it maximized available program funds to prioritize 71 ongoing scholars from the poorest households and those belonging to the special equity group. The remaining financial requirements totaling ₱56,663,250 will be covered by the HEDF. The use of the HEDF is consistent with the 2026 General Appropriations Act, which directs CHED to consider the full requirements of existing scholars when programming the fund to ensure continuity of their financial support. CHED Chairperson Shirley C. Agrupis said the Commission remains committed to helping current scholars complete their degrees while preparing more medical technologists and pharmacists to meet the country's healthcare needs. For AY 2025-2026, 13 MTP-SP scholars are expected to graduate, including four Medical Technology/Medical Laboratory Science students and nine Pharmacy students. After passing their respective licensure examinations, the graduates will be required to render one year of government service for every year they received the scholarship, in accordance with Department of Health guidelines. The return-service requirement is intended to help augment the supply of licensed medical technologists and pharmacists in the public health sector. The MTP-SP provides financial assistance to qualified Filipino students pursuing Bachelor of Science degrees in Medical Technology/Medical Laboratory Science and Pharmacy at participating higher education institutions.

Pagcor releases ₱65.6 million in aid for typhoon, flood-hit communities. State-run Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corp. (Pagcor) has released an initial ₱65.6 million in relief assistance to communities in Luzon and Metro Manila affected by Tropical Cyclones Luis and Maymay and the enhanced southwest monsoon, or “ habagat. ” In a statement on Thursday, Aug. 13, Pagcor said the assistance consisted of 47,192 relief items, including 23,596 food packs worth ₱28.91 million and an equal number of non-food packs worth ₱36.69 million. Pagcor Chairman and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Alejandro H. Tengco said the agency has been distributing relief packs to affected communities since Aug. 8 as part of its continuing disaster response efforts. “Calamities cause immediate burden on families, particularly when basic needs become difficult to secure. Pagcor is committed to providing timely assistance to communities that need them most,” Tengco said. Since last week, Pagcor’s relief operations team has been delivering assistance to areas affected by heavy rains and flooding. The relief goods have either reached or are on their way to Bulacan, La Union, Baguio City, Isabela, Nueva Ecija, Cavite, and Rizal, as well as parts of Pangasinan, Quezon, Batangas, Camarines Norte, Abra, Laguna, and Pampanga provinces. In Metro Manila, assistance has also been allocated to Parañaque City and Marikina City. Heavy rains associated with the tropical cyclones and “ habagat ” caused severe flooding in Luzon and Metro Manila, disrupting classes and government operations. Tengco said Pagcor would continue coordinating with government partners to extend assistance to communities affected by calamities. “We will continue to stand with our kababayans in times of need. Through our continuing disaster response efforts, Pagcor will do its part to help affected communities recover and get back on their feet,” Tengco added.

Marcos visits Las Piñas flood evacuees, leads aid distribution. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) Secretary Rex Gatchalian checked on 155 families displaced by flooding in Las Piñas City on Tuesday, Aug. 11, after inspecting flood‑mitigation efforts at Alido Bridge in Barangay Zapote. The families were temporarily staying at the Verdant Covered Court in Barangay Pamplona Tres after an overflowing river caused floodwaters to rise to dangerous levels in several parts of the city. Following the inspection at Alido Bridge, Marcos proceeded to the evacuation center with Gatchalian to personally assess the condition of the displaced families and their immediate needs. The President led the distribution of food and non‑food items (FNFIs), including family food packs, sleeping kits, clothing kits, and maternity kits. Marcos also inquired about the families’ situation while they remain unable to return home and determined what additional assistance they may require. Las Piñas City Mayor Imelda Aguilar joined Marcos and Gatchalian during the visit, along with DSWD Disaster Response Management Group Assistant Secretary Irene Dumlao, DSWD Field Office–National Capital Region Regional Director Atty. Michael Joseph Lorico, and Assistant Regional Director for Operations Bienvenido Barbosa Jr. The visit was part of the government’s continuing response to communities affected by flooding brought about by continuous heavy rains.

Personal social media accounts do not exempt teachers, school personnel from professional standards — DepEd. Using personal social media accounts does not exempt teachers and other school personnel from professional and ethical standards, the Department of Education (DepEd) reminded its personnel. This came after the agency received reports of posts that may not be consistent with DepEd’s standards of professionalism. In a memorandum dated Aug. 11, DepEd Undersecretary Fatima Lipp Panontongan, who also serves as Chief of Staff of the Office of the Secretary, reminded DepEd personnel to exercise professionalism, prudence, and sound judgment online. “This Office has received reports of social media posts involving teachers and other school personnel that may not be consistent with the standards of professionalism expected of DepEd personnel,” Panontongan stated. “These reports highlight the need to exercise appropriate judgment and responsibility in the use of social media, particularly where online activities involve learners, classroom activities, school premises, or otherwise arise from the performance of official functions,” she added. DepEd stressed that professional obligations continue to apply even when personnel post through their personal accounts. “The use of personal social media accounts does not, by itself, dispense with the professional and ethical standards applicable to DepEd personnel, particularly where the content is connected with the performance of their official functions, identifies or represents them as DepEd personnel, or involves learners, school activities, or school premises,” Panontongan said. As such, teachers and other personnel who directly interact with learners were told to exercise particular care when creating or publishing social media content involving students or classroom activities. The education department pointed out that teachers occupy positions of trust and exercise authority and influence over learners. “Thus, they are expected to maintain appropriate professional boundaries and to exercise sound professional judgment where content features learners under their supervision or makes use of classroom activities or school premises,” said Panontongan. The agency likewise reminded personnel to exercise caution when sharing posts or other content and to remain mindful of DepEd’s reputation and honor. DepEd cited Order No. 049, series of 2022, which contains provisions on the responsible use of social media, and Order No. 006, series of 2026, which applies learner-protection measures in physical and virtual settings. The latter also requires safeguards against the unauthorized use, access, or disclosure of learners’ personally identifiable information, including through social media.

Valenzuela gov’t, DPWH move to rehabilitate damaged Maysan Road. The Valenzuela City government and the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) have started addressing the damaged portions of Maysan Road, with P81 million earmarked for the first phase of its rehabilitation. Mayor Weslie “Wes” Gatchalian and DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon inspected the road on Thursday, Aug. 13, to assess the extent of the damage and identify sections requiring immediate intervention. Workers also carried out temporary road repairs and pothole-filling operations during the inspection. The city government said several portions of Maysan Road have deteriorated over time due to recurring typhoons, heavy rains, flooding, and the frequent passage of heavy trucks. Dizon said the recent continuous rains brought by the southwest monsoon, or habagat, further damaged the road. The DPWH said the first phase of rehabilitation, funded with P81 million, is expected to be completed within six months. The local government and the DPWH are also discussing the possible extension of truck ban hours to give workers more time to carry out repair works. It added that the temporary repairs will continue while preparations are underway for the full rehabilitation of the road.

Soft-drink delivery van falls on its side in QC. A delivery van loaded with soft drinks tipped over while turning at the EDSA-Aurora Boulevard intersection in Cubao, Quezon City, Thursday morning, Aug. 13. The van’s driver, “Jemar,” said it suddenly tilted as he was turning at the intersection while they were on their way to Manila from Bagumbayan, Quezon City. Jemar and his helper were the only two people in the van, and neither was reported injured. The van occupied one lane of EDSA northbound leading to the westbound lane, but motorists could still pass through the area. Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) enforcers responded to the scene and managed traffic while trying to upright the van. They failed to immediately move the vehicle because of its heavy load of soft drinks, prompting them to remove the bottles by hand to lighten its load. Some MMDA personnel said the bottles may not have been properly secured or tightly packed, causing the weight to shift to one side as the van turned from EDSA northbound toward the westbound lane. The van also hit several concrete barriers during the incident, according to authorities. As of 12:30 p.m., authorities had cleared the EDSA-Cubao intersection, and police said the van would be brought to QCPD Traffic Sector 4 for investigation.

DOE, BARMM fast-track Sulu Sea petroleum deals, native hydrogen rules. The Department of Energy (DOE) and Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) are fast-tracking joint management arrangements for newly awarded petroleum contracts in Sulu Sea while establishing a regulatory framework for native hydrogen exploration in the region. In a statement on Thursday, Aug. 13, the DOE and BARMM’s Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources, and Energy (MENRE) said they are finalizing a joint circular that would allow them to co-manage newly awarded petroleum service contracts (SCs) 80 and 81. These contracts are under the consortium of Australia’s Triangle Energy (Global) Ltd., the United Kingdom’s (UK) Sunda Energy Plc, PXP Energy Corp., and local company The Philodrill Corp. They would allow Manuel V. Pangilinan-led PXP to expand its petroleum activities in Sulu Sea. In addition, the DOE and MENRE are expected to adopt a regulatory framework for native hydrogen exploration and development in BARMM. This would mark the country’s second native hydrogen initiative, following exploration work kicked off by United States (US)-based Koloma Inc. in Pangasinan and Zambales provinces. Beyond resource development, the DOE is gradually transferring power and electrification functions to MENRE to strengthen BARMM’s capacity to manage its own energy sector. Both agencies are also drafting the proposed BARMM Energy Code to set up long-term rules and policies for the region. To close remaining access gaps, the DOE and MENRE are also mapping out an electrification plan targeting BARMM’s isolated and off-grid areas, including the hard-to-reach Turtle Islands. DOE Undersecretary Giovanni Bacordo said these developments would help accelerate and improve the regional energy landscape. “Total electrification must mean reaching communities where providing electricity is most difficult. Our objective is both improving electrification figures and making sure that geography does not hinder Bangsamoro family to electricity access,” Bacordo said. - Gabriell Christel Galang

Anne Curtis gets real about her skin concerns. In front of the camera, Anne Curtis is the embodiment of a dyosa (goddess), but behind the scenes, the actress and Cetaphil ambassador, just like all of us, also deals with skin concerns that change with age, lifestyle, and even the weather. In an interview with Manila Bulletin Lifestyle during the launch of Cetaphil’s National Healthy Skin Mission 2026 on Aug. 7, Anne opened up about how her relationship with skincare has evolved, from being content with a little moisturizer to becoming more conscious about sunscreen, serums, and caring for her skin. “As time changes, so does your skin,” she said. She also recalled that when she was younger, she would be happy with just a little moisturizer. Sunscreen and serums were not yet part of her routine. As she got older, however, she learned to recognize the products and ingredients her skin needed. Among the concerns Anne has learned to embrace is her freckles and dry skin. She shared that she is also still working on melasma, which became more noticeable after giving birth and can be aggravated by sun exposure. “I used to be conscious about these things. But now, it's so easy to gain access to how you can repair your skin,” she said, adding that better access to skincare education has helped take away the fear and embarrassment surrounding certain skin conditions. Her own routine has also become more consistent. The “It’s Showtime” host said she now makes sure to remove her makeup even when she is tired, followed by double cleansing with a gentle cleanser. She then uses toner, serums, and moisturizer. But she also keeps things realistic. “If there are nights that I'm also so tired, I lessen the routine. Remover. Wash. No more toner straight to moisturizer then sleep,” she shared with a laugh. During the day, one step remains non-negotiable: sunscreen. “After moisturizer, sunscreen. I wish I had learned that sooner,” she said. As an in-demand celebrity, Anne travels a lot. She has learned to also adjust her routine depending on the weather and where she is traveling. In colder countries, she adds more layers of moisturizer and sunscreen, while in warmer weather, she opts for products that feel less sticky. When asked about her favorite Cetaphil products, she shared that these are the serums, the Healthy Bright Radiance line, Ceramide Barrier Lotion, and a moisturizer with SPF. She particularly likes the Ceramide Barrier Lotion because her skin has been especially dry lately. “You don’t need to follow the hype,” she said when discussing how she chooses skincare products. For Ann, it is more important to find products that work for her rather than simply following trends. That philosophy also guides the advice she gives to younger skincare users. Anne encourages children and preteens to use gentle cleansers, especially after swimming, and to make sunscreen a habit. For adults, she recommends finding what works for their skin and following trusted dermatologists online instead of blindly following influencer recommendations. After six years as a Cetaphil ambassador, she continues to see value in the brand’s National Healthy Skin Mission, particularly because it serves as an annual reminder to prioritize skin health. “I think it’s a good thing to be educated and informed through this kind of program. It takes away that fear or shame about certain skin conditions that you have.”

ALI dragged Ayala’s profits down, but two businesses stepped up. Ayala Corp., the country’s oldest conglomerate, posted a seven percent decline in first-half core net income to ₱22.1 billion, squeezed by weaker contributions from real estate unit Ayala Land Inc. and reduced holdings in key affiliate companies. The Zobel-led group reported to the Philippine Stock Exchange that earnings growth at Globe Telecom Inc. and AC Energy and Infrastructure Corp. (ACEIC), alongside steady results from Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI), helped temper the impact of lower property income and diminished non-operating receipts. Aggregate earnings from emerging businesses also contributed positively. Non-operating income took a hit primarily due to lower dividend payments from Manila Water Co., following the full settlement of divested preferred shares, as well as a scaled-back stake in Mynt after Mitsubishi Corp. acquired a position in AM 50 Ventures Inc. last year. Including one-off items, Ayala’s reported net income slipped two percent to ₱22.9 billion. BPI maintained a flat net profit of ₱32.8 billion, as robust revenue generation was countered by elevated operating expenditures and credit provisions. Globe’s normalized net profit expanded 10 percent to ₱11 billion, propelled by record gross service revenues. ACEIC, the parent entity of ACEN Corp., nearly doubled its net income to ₱4.9 billion from ₱2.5 billion a year earlier. The boost came from stronger thermal power plant operations, higher net interest income, and foreign exchange gains. The conglomerate emphasized its resilient stance amid broader market instability, highlighting conservative leverage and solid liquidity. Consolidated cash balances reached ₱75.6 billion, while parent-level cash stood at ₱19.9 billion. “A well-diversified portfolio coupled with good traction from initiatives undertaken over the past few years have produced solid results even in a period of geopolitical and macroeconomic challenges,” Ayala Chief Executive Officer Cezar P. Consing said in a statement. “Seeing how our portfolio has performed in a challenging environment gives us confidence of the considerable value that can be created in a more benign environment,” he added. Among its non-listed ventures, AC Health grew revenues by 25 percent to ₱7.5 billion. Expanding operations led to higher marketing and staffing overheads, widening its net loss to ₱167 million from ₱64 million previously. Its provider group—comprising hospitals and clinics—logged a 32 percent revenue jump driven by rising patient volume, higher average client spending, and new traction from the Healthway Cancer Care Hospital and FEU-NRMF. Its pharmaceutical arm saw revenues rise 13 percent, buoyed by store network expansion for Generika and government contracts. ACMobility swung to a core net loss of ₱57 million from a ₱34 million profit a year ago, excluding equity earnings from Honda Cars Philippines Inc. Margins were pressured by higher inventory costs triggered by weaker peso and slower demand for Kia and Isuzu units. However, total unit sales advanced 25 percent to 25,048 vehicles, lifted by surging demand for BYD electric vehicles. This expanded ACMobility’s market share by 2.9 percentage points to 10.9 percent, making it the country’s third-largest automotive distributor. Integrated Micro-Electronics Inc. recorded a 50 percent increase in net income—excluding losses from Via Optronics—to $14 million from $9.4 million, fueled by revenue expansion and wider profit margins. Meanwhile, AC Logistics cut its net loss by 58 percent to ₱264 million from ₱631 million, benefiting from cost discipline, operational adjustments, and an improved revenue mix following a strategic reorganization. (James A. Loyola)

Sarines-led North, South rekindle rivalry in ICTSI JPGT Finals. A recent national championship showdown gets a compelling sequel when the ICTSI Elite Junior PGT Finals blasts off Tuesday, Aug. 18, with North’s Lisa Sarines and Team South’s Tashanah Balangauan and Precious Zaragosa renewing their rivalry in the girls’ 15-18 division at the Pueblo de Oro Golf and Country Club. Sarines comes into the Ryder Cup-style showdown with bragging rights firmly in hand after dominating Balangauan and Zaragosa in the National Stroke Play Championship at Pradera Verde. But while the North ace proved her mettle in a pressure-packed individual battle, Zaragosa has since shown signs of a strong bounce-back, particularly in head-to-head competition. Zaragosa emerged as the top performer among the three in the National Match Play Championship, advancing all the way to the final before settling for runner-up honors to champion Grace Quintanilla. Sarines, meanwhile, placed third, while Balangauan also saw action in the tournament. The three, however, did not cross paths, leaving Zaragosa without a chance to face Sarines directly. Still, Zaragosa’s deep run in match play provides a timely boost heading into the team showdown, where she and Balangauan will look to turn the tables on Sarines and the North squad. And with the South players boasting greater familiarity with Pueblo de Oro, the rematch could take on a much different complexion from their previous encounter.
